content: Access to up-to-date information is essential for prosthetics and orthotics professionals. This can be achieved through regularly updated online or offline resources, such as the WHO Hinari e-Granary system and open-source journals. To ensure personnel have access to these resources, support in the form of computer hardware and software can be provided. A culture of evidence-based practice can be fostered by sharing case studies and developing treatment protocols grounded in evidence. Mentorship programs, either in-person or via e-health platforms, can pair mentors with personnel to analyze case studies and enhance their skills. This approach to continuing professional development (CPD) helps embed new knowledge and techniques after short courses. For instance, a mentor may supervise a series of prosthetics and orthotics treatments until the mentee is proficient and confident in applying new methods. Prosthetics and orthotics personnel must remain committed to lifelong learning, CPD, and reflective practice. A mandatory amount of CPD per year should be a condition of employment. Experienced personnel should engage in annual professional development planning, identifying their CPD needs and collaborating with employers and professional associations to implement individualized plans. Training courses in prosthetics and orthotics provide foundational knowledge for practice, but no graduate will possess all the skills required to master every sub-field. Expertise is developed over time through daily practice, collaboration with colleagues and mentors, and participation in courses and seminars. Roles within the profession evolve to meet service needs and complement the competencies of other rehabilitation team members. In larger units, personnel may specialize in narrower areas, such as upper-limb prosthetics, diabetic footwear, or sports injuries, enhancing proficiency and service quality while reducing the need for extensive cross-training. Role development within prosthetics and orthotics can extend beyond traditional boundaries. Professionals may take on tasks within multidisciplinary teams, assume management responsibilities, or pursue advanced degrees. Technicians may receive additional training to perform some roles of prosthetists or orthotists under proper supervision. Role development increases productivity, service quality, and workforce efficiency, while also serving as a motivational factor for individuals by offering recognition and specialized responsibilities. Workforce planning is critical to ensure the appropriate number of personnel with the right competencies at primary, secondary, and tertiary service levels. This involves assessing service needs, calculating personnel requirements, profiling the existing workforce, and addressing gaps between current supply and future demand. Workforce development plans should align with national census cycles and consider other disciplines contributing to prosthetics and orthotics services, such as physicians and rehabilitation professionals. Retention of personnel is vital, given the significant financial investment in training and mentoring. Strategies to retain professionals include selecting students genuinely interested in the field, providing equitable recognition, offering career opportunities, ensuring competitive salaries and benefits, and fostering a positive working environment. Migration of professionals from lowto high-income countries or rural to urban areas poses challenges, particularly in lowand middle-income countries. Employment bonds and codes of conduct for recruitment and retention can help ensure that investments in training benefit the intended regions. Professional regulation is necessary to protect users from harm. Prosthetics and orthotics clinicians should be regulated by an independent state body that maintains a register of practicing professionals. This ensures adherence to high standards of training, skills, ethics, and conduct. Technicians and other technical personnel should work under the supervision of certified clinicians, who are accountable for their conduct. Professional recognition is crucial for motivation, retention, and development. Awareness of the distinct roles and titles of prosthetists, orthotists, associates, and technicians in healthcare provision should be raised. Recognition should also be integrated into local career structures, with employment conditions aligned with those of other healthcare professions.
